## Recap quiz: Session 6 in five questions

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 8 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A crude OR (odds ratio) is 2.1. The adjusted OR is 1.4. What happened?
- HR (hazard ratio) 0.85, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.20: a clear benefit?
- Lactate is missing for 15% of patients. Name one way to handle it
- Kaplan-Meier curve: what does a 'censored' patient mean?
- The FLUID-ICU question you chose (Q1 to Q5): what is its main result? Answer in the chat
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Answers

- Confounding: part of the crude link came from severity
- No: the CI includes 1
- Complete-case analysis, or multiple imputation with a sensitivity analysis
- Left the study alive. Outcome unknown after that
- From your results pack
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone re-activated: adjustment, CIs, missing data, survival
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap (19:30-19:40, including 1 minute of welcome and the 'Today' slide). Start by reading two or three answers to the Session 6 exit question (you read them during the week) and correct any misunderstanding.

Questions 1-4 are open questions. Read each one, give 30 seconds, then call on two or three people to answer, microphone on. Reveal the answer panel after each question. Spend longest where answers differ.

Question 1 links straight to today's writing: in the Results we report both crude and adjusted estimates (STROBE item 16), and in the Discussion we explain why they differ.

Question 5 goes in the chat. This is the number each participant will write about after the break. Anyone who has not yet chosen a question chooses one today (Q1 to Q5, results packs sent before the session).
:::

## The protocol: your study's building plan

::: {.neu-intro}
Protocol = the full written plan of a study, approved before the first patient. Trial checklist: SPIRIT 2025.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Who and what]{.neu-card-title}

- Title page
- Title, version, date
- Registration number
- Team, roles, funding
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Why]{.neu-card-title}

- Proposal Part 1
- Problem and rationale
- Question (PICO)
- Aim, objectives, hypothesis
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[How]{.neu-card-title}

- Proposal Parts 2-3
- Design, setting, participants
- Exposure, outcomes
- Sample size, data, analysis plan
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Protect and share]{.neu-card-title}

- Proposal Part 4 (today)
- Ethics approval, consent
- Confidentiality, data safety
- Publication plan
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Your four proposal parts are the skeleton of a protocol.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: a protocol is the full written plan of the study, written and approved before the first patient is enrolled. SPIRIT 2025 (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) is the international checklist for what a trial protocol should contain. Observational studies follow the same logic.

Walk the four cards: who and what (title page, registration, team, funding), why (Part 1), how (Parts 2 and 3), protect and share (Part 4, today). PICO = Population, Intervention or exposure, Comparison, Outcome.

Changes after approval are made as formal amendments, approved before they are applied, never quietly.

Running example: Paper 1 says its protocol and statistical analysis plan were registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04947904) before the first patient. That is what lets a reader check the authors did what they planned.

Poll: which part of your own proposal is weakest right now? Expected: How (sample size or analysis plan). Reassure: the proposal template (Course/Templates/Research\_Proposal\_Template) follows exactly this order.
:::

## Two rule books: Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2024)]{.neu-card-title}

- Participants' rights and well-being first
- Protocol approved by an ethics committee
- Free, informed consent
- Risks minimised and justified
- Privacy and confidentiality
- Register first, publish all results
:::
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Good Clinical Practice (GCP: ICH E6(R3), 2025)]{.neu-card-title}

- Qualified, trained team
- Quality built in by design
- Clear, feasible protocol
- Checks in proportion to the risk
- Reliable, traceable data
- Clear roles and responsibilities
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Helsinki says why we protect participants. GCP says how we run a trial well.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, latest revision October 2024) is the ethical foundation for research with people. Its core: the rights and interests of the individual participant come before the goal of new knowledge. A protocol approved by an independent research ethics committee before the study starts. Free, informed consent, risks minimised and justified, privacy protected. Every study registered before the first participant and all results made public, including negative and inconclusive ones.

The 2024 revision speaks of 'participants' rather than 'subjects', strengthens the protection of vulnerable groups and of people who cannot consent, and stresses scientific integrity.

ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice (ICH = International Council for Harmonisation, adopted January 2025) is the international quality standard for clinical trials. Its spirit applies to every study.

Misconception: 'GCP is only for drug companies'. Paper 1, an academic ICU trial, states its analyses followed ICH-GCP.

Poll: which of these 12 points would be hardest in our unit? Typical answer: reliable data (charts incomplete) or protected time.
:::

## The ethics-committee journey: approval before data

::: {.neu-intro}
Plan 1 to 3 months. Questions and revisions from the committee are normal.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Prepare]{.neu-step-label}

- Protocol
- Consent form
- Case report form (CRF)
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Review]{.neu-step-label}

- Scientific or department review first
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Submit]{.neu-step-label}

- Dossier to the research ethics committee
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Decide]{.neu-step-label}

- Exempt, expedited or full committee
- The committee decides
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Approve]{.neu-step-label}

- Approval letter with number and date
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#8A99A3"}
[Start]{.neu-step-label}

- Trials: register first
- Then the first patient
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** No approval letter, no data collection: not even 'just a few patients'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the six steps left to right. Most institutions want a scientific or department review first. Then the dossier goes to the research ethics committee (also called IRB, institutional review board, or IEC, independent ethics committee).

The dossier: protocol, participant information and consent form, case report form (CRF), investigator CVs and GCP training records, budget and insurance where required.

Review types: some low-risk studies are exempt or get an expedited review. Trials and anything with more than minimal risk go to the full committee. Your committee decides the category, not you.

During the study: amendments, adverse-event reports, progress and final reports go to the committee.

Misconception to correct: 'we can collect data now and ask for approval later'. Committees cannot approve retrospectively, and journals will reject the paper.

Running example: Paper 1 gives its committee name and approval number in the Methods. Paper 2 gives the IRB approval number in its Declarations.
:::

## Register before the first participant

::: {.neu-intro}
The order: protocol, ethics approval, registration, first participant.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Clinical trials]{.neu-card-title}

- **[Mandatory]{style="color:#C0392B"}**
- ClinicalTrials.gov or another who primary registry
- Paper 1: registered 1 July 2021, first patient September 2021
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Systematic reviews]{.neu-card-title}

- **[Expected]{style="color:#D9822B"}**
- PROSPERO, the register for review protocols
- Before data extraction
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Observational studies]{.neu-card-title}

- **[Recommended]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
- For example on ClinicalTrials.gov
- Check the journal and local rules
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Trials: no registration before the first patient, no publication.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: registration puts the study's existence, design and primary outcome on a public record before anyone is enrolled. It prevents hidden negative studies and outcome switching.

Clinical trials: registration is mandatory. Journals that follow ICMJE (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors) will not publish a trial that was not registered before the first participant, and many countries require it by law. Use ClinicalTrials.gov or another who primary registry. The WHO ICTRP (International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) searches all of them at once. It is a search portal, not a registry itself.

Systematic reviews: register the protocol on PROSPERO before data extraction. Many journals expect it.

Observational studies: registration is encouraged rather than required. The Declaration of Helsinki asks for every study with human participants to be registered.

Running example: Paper 1 was registered as NCT04947904 on 1 July 2021, and the first patient was enrolled in September 2021, so registration was prospective. Its registration number is in the abstract.

Ask (call on two or three people, microphone on): does your own study need registration? Expected: trials yes, most cohort proposals 'recommended'. A short poll on four scenarios is in the Extra slides if you have time.
:::

## Informed consent: four essentials

::: {.neu-intro}
Consent is a conversation, not a signature.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Informed]{.neu-card-title}

- Purpose and what will happen
- Risks, benefits, alternatives
- How data are protected
- Who to contact
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Understood]{.neu-card-title}

- Plain, local language
- Time to ask questions
- Teach-back: 'tell me in your words'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Voluntary]{.neu-card-title}

- No pressure
- Free to refuse or withdraw
- Care is not affected
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Documented]{.neu-card-title}

- Signed and dated form
- A copy for the participant
- Re-consent if the study changes
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** If the patient cannot explain the study back to you, consent is not informed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: valid consent needs all four: information, understanding, voluntariness and a record.

Patients often ask the nurses and other team members afterwards 'what did I sign?', so this is everybody's job, not only the investigator's.

Withdrawal: participants may leave at any time without giving a reason and without any effect on their care. Running example: in Paper 1, two control patients withdrew consent and were not analysed. That is the right being respected, and it is why the trial analysed 48 of 50.

Common mistake: a consent form written at university reading level, in a language the family does not read fluently. Ask the committee for its template (there is also one in Course/Templates/Informed\_Consent\_Template).

Ask (call on two or three people, microphone on): who would take consent in your own study, and when? Expected answer: a trained team member who is not the treating doctor under time pressure, if possible.
:::

## Consent in the ICU: when the patient cannot decide

![](images/figures/sat4/icu_consent.png){.neu-fig}

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Patient, then legal representative, then deferred consent (only if approved).
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the real-life ICU problem: most of our patients are sedated, delirious or in shock when they become eligible. This flowchart stays a picture because its branches are the message.

Read the flowchart left to right. 1) Can the patient decide now? Then the patient consents. 2) If not, a legally authorised representative (surrogate: usually family, as defined by local law) consents, and the patient is asked again when able. 3) If no representative can be reached in time and the treatment cannot wait, research may proceed only if the protocol explains why and the ethics committee approved this emergency procedure in advance. Consent to continue is then sought as soon as possible. This is 'deferred consent'. The 2024 Declaration of Helsinki allows exactly this, under these conditions.

Paper 1 used this: written consent from the patient or legal surrogate 'before randomization or as soon as possible thereafter' (page 3).

Paper 2 is different: a registry using routine data. The committee waived individual consent and the data were de-identified before analysis (page 8).

Local law decides who may act as representative and whether deferred consent is allowed. Check with your committee before you write the protocol.

Ask: if a family refuses after the patient was enrolled under deferred consent, what happens? Expected: the patient leaves the study. Whether data already collected may be used depends on the approved protocol and what the family agrees to.
:::

## Worked example: who consents for these three ICU patients?

::: {.neu-intro}
Walk each patient through the flowchart on the previous slide.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Mr A, 54]{.neu-card-title}

- Pneumonia, awake, oriented
- Eligible for a fluid trial
- **[Patient consents]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Mrs B, 71]{.neu-card-title}

- Septic shock, sedated
- Daughter at the bedside
- **[Representative consents. Ask Mrs B when awake]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Mr C, 38]{.neu-card-title}

- Septic shock at 03:00, no family yet
- Treatment cannot wait, committee approved
- **[Deferred consent: ask as soon as possible]{style="color:#D9822B"}**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The pathway and the timing are written in the protocol before patient 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example, whole class. For each patient, call on someone to answer before you reveal the bottom line (click through slowly).

Mr A: capacity present, so the patient decides.

Mrs B: lacks capacity now. The legally authorised representative (here the daughter, if local law allows) consents. Mrs B is asked to continue when she regains capacity, and she may withdraw.

Mr C: no representative in time and treatment cannot wait. Deferred consent applies only if the protocol describes it and the committee approved it. Seek consent from family or patient as soon as possible. Paper 1 used this route.

Misconception: 'the treating doctor can consent for the patient'. No. The treating doctor is not the representative.
:::

## Confidentiality: de-identify before you analyse

| Item | Before: identifiable | After: de-identified |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Name | Ana P. | Study code SEP-001 |
| Hospital number | 1084521 | Removed |
| Date of birth | 12/03/1956 | Age 68 |
| Admission date | 14/03/2024 | Month 03/2024 |
| Fluid balance, ml/kg | +35 | +35 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Names stay on the ward. Only study codes travel. The key file (code = identity) is locked and kept separately. Beware very small groups (n \< 5).
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: confidentiality is protected by design, not by good intentions.

Before: direct identifiers such as name, hospital number, exact date of birth, address, phone, photos. After: a study code, age instead of birth date, month instead of exact dates, and only the variables in your data dictionary. The invented example row is one patient before and after.

The key file that links codes to identities is kept separately, password-protected and locked, with access for one or two named people only.

Beware indirect identification: 'the only 19-year-old with ECMO in March' is identifiable even without a name. Report very small groups with care.

Practical rules: no patient data on personal phones, messaging apps, private email or public cloud and AI tools. Encrypted, institution-approved storage only.

Running example: Paper 2 states that patient information was anonymised and de-identified before analysis.

Ask (call on two or three people, microphone on): where would the key file of your own study live? Expected answer: an institution-approved, password-protected location, not a USB stick in a pocket.
:::

## Worked example: the ethics paragraph for a cohort like FLUID-ICU

::: {.neu-intro}
FLUID-ICU is simulated. If it were real, this is what the paper would say.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Approval]{.neu-card-title}

- Ethics committee of each ICU
- Approval number and date
- Before data collection
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Consent]{.neu-card-title}

- Routine data, minimal risk
- Committee may waive consent (as in Paper 2)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Confidentiality]{.neu-card-title}

- Study codes only
- Key file kept in each ICU
- Data de-identified before analysis
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Registration and sharing]{.neu-card-title}

- Registration recommended
- Data-sharing statement
- Data dictionary shared
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Your manuscript's ethics paragraph answers four questions in four sentences.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example linking 7.1 to the manuscript. Make clear FLUID-ICU is a simulated teaching dataset with no real approval, so in their manuscripts participants write: 'This analysis used a simulated teaching dataset. No ethics approval or consent was required.' In a real cohort the paragraph would read like the four cards.

Model sentence (real study): 'The study was approved by the ethics committees of the four participating hospitals (number, date), which waived individual consent because data were collected during routine care and analysed after de-identification.'

Ask: where does this paragraph go? Expected: the Methods. Most journals also ask for it in a 'Declarations' section.
:::

## Feasibility: five honest questions

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Timeline]{.neu-card-title}

- Ethics alone: 1 to 3 months
- Recruitment takes longer than planned
- Draw a simple timeline (Gantt chart)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Budget]{.neu-card-title}

- Staff time
- Materials and tests
- Publication fee
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[People]{.neu-card-title}

- Who collects data at night?
- Who analyses?
- Protected time?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Recruitment]{.neu-card-title}

- Paper 1: 1201 screened, 50 randomised (4%)
- 17 months, 3 ICUs
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Data]{.neu-card-title}

- Recorded routinely?
- How much will be missing?
- Paper 2: no diuretic data
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Count the eligible patients in your unit before you write the sample size.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the five cards. Timeline: ethics approval alone can take 1-3 months. Recruitment always takes longer than planned. Budget: name the headings even if the amounts are small. People: who collects data on night shifts and weekends, who analyses, and is there protected time? Recruitment: Paper 1 screened 1201 patients in three ICUs over 17 months to randomise 50 (about 4%). Most eligible-looking patients are not eligible or not enrolled. Data: is the variable already recorded routinely? Paper 2 could not study diuretics because the registry never recorded them.

Rule of thumb: count how many patients meeting your criteria your unit saw last year, then assume you will enrol a fraction of them.

Poll: which card is the biggest risk for your own study? Expected answers: recruitment and people (night-shift data collection).

This is the only feasibility slide in Level 1. Do not go deeper.
:::

## 7.2  \|  20 minutes

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Research integrity
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
Honest data, honest credit, honest use of AI
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 7.2 (20:10-20:30). Six slides (about 2.5 minutes each), then the 5-minute scenario poll at 20:25.

Tone: this is not about catching cheats. Most integrity problems start as small shortcuts under pressure: a missing value 'filled in', an outlier 'cleaned', a boss added as author. We want people to recognise the slope early.

Link to the manuscript: every participant's draft needs an authorship, conflicts-of-interest, data-availability and AI-use statement.
:::

## Research misconduct: fabrication, falsification, plagiarism

::: {.neu-intro}
FFP = the three forms of research misconduct. An honest error is not misconduct: correct it openly.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Fabrication]{.neu-card-title}

- Making up data or patients
- Example: day-3 fluid balances entered 'from memory'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Falsification]{.neu-card-title}

- Changing or leaving out data to fit the story
- Example: dropping two 'odd' patients who weaken the result
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Plagiarism]{.neu-card-title}

- Using others' words or ideas without credit
- Example: a copied paragraph, cited but without quotation marks
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Missing data are reported as missing: never invented, never quietly removed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: the three classic forms of research misconduct (FFP).

Fabrication: making up data or patients (e.g. filling day-3 fluid balances 'from memory' because the chart is lost).

Falsification: changing, selecting or leaving out data, images or results so the story looks better (e.g. dropping two 'odd' patients after seeing they weaken the result).

Plagiarism: using other people's words, ideas or figures without credit, including copying a paragraph with a citation but without quotation marks.

Honest error is not misconduct, but it must be corrected openly (a correction or erratum).

Link to Session 5: the data-quality plan (range checks, pre-specified rules for outliers) is what protects you from accidental falsification.

Poll: which of these three is the most common in student theses? Expected answer: plagiarism, often copy-paste in the introduction. Similarity-check software will find it.
:::

## Also off-limits: tricks that distort the record

::: {.neu-intro}
One study should tell one complete, honest story.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Duplicate publication]{.neu-card-title}

- Same results published twice
- The second paper does not say so
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Salami slicing]{.neu-card-title}

- One study cut into thin papers
- Done to multiply publications
- The reader never sees the whole
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Selective reporting]{.neu-card-title}

- Only the 'significant' outcomes reported
- Primary outcome switched after seeing the data
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Register first, pre-specify the primary outcome, report all of it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: these practices distort the evidence that doctors and guideline panels rely on.

Duplicate publication counts the same patients twice in a meta-analysis and can exaggerate an effect. A legitimate secondary paper is fine if it is clearly cross-referenced and adds something new.

Salami slicing: e.g. mortality in one paper, kidney injury in another and ICU stay in a third, from the same cohort, each without mentioning the others.

Selective reporting and outcome switching are why trials must be registered with one primary outcome before the first patient. Running example: Paper 1 registered its protocol at ClinicalTrials.gov on 1 July 2021, before recruitment began in September 2021, and reported its negative primary outcome plainly in the abstract. That is good practice.

Ask: Paper 1's primary outcome was negative. Why does it matter that it was published at all? Expected: publication bias. If only positive trials appear, the literature overstates benefit.
:::

## Who is an author? The four ICMJE criteria

::: {.neu-intro}
ICMJE = International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. An author meets all four.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[1  Substantial work]{.neu-card-title}

- Idea, design, data, analysis or interpretation
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[2  Writing]{.neu-card-title}

- Drafted or critically revised the manuscript
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[3  Approval]{.neu-card-title}

- Approved the final version
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[4  Accountable]{.neu-card-title}

- Answers for all of the work
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#C0392B"}
[Not all four?]{.neu-card-title}

- Thank them in the Acknowledgements
- Gift author: named, did not do the work
- Ghost author: did the work, not named
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** All four criteria, for every author. Decide the list at the start.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) requires all four criteria for authorship: 1) substantial contribution to conception or design, or to acquisition, analysis or interpretation of data, 2) drafting or critically revising the work, 3) final approval of the version to be published, 4) agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work.

Anyone who contributed but does not meet all four goes in the Acknowledgements (data collectors, a colleague who checked adherence, the department head who provided support).

Gift author: a name added for seniority or friendship. Ghost author: someone who did the work (often a junior or a paid writer) but is not named. Both are misconduct.

Running example: Paper 2 is published 'on behalf of' a study group, and the group members are listed in the Acknowledgements. That is a correct way to credit a large network.

Poll: data collection alone, is that enough for authorship? Expected answer: no, not without criteria 2, 3 and 4.

Practical tip: agree the author list and order in writing at the protocol stage and revisit it before submission. CRediT (who did what) is in the Extra slides.
:::

## Conflicts of interest and funding: declare them all

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Financial interests]{.neu-card-title}

- Consultancy, speaker fees
- Grants, travel support
- Shares, patents
- Employment
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Non-financial interests]{.neu-card-title}

- Personal relationships
- Role in a guideline panel
- Strong prior beliefs
- Academic rivalry
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Funding statement]{.neu-card-title}

- Who paid, grant number
- Role of the funder in design, analysis, writing and the decision to publish
- Paper 2: the funder had no role
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A declared interest is information. A hidden one is a scandal.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: a conflict (competing) interest is anything that could be seen to influence your judgement, financial or not. Having one is common and not wrong. Hiding it is.

Every author completes the journal's disclosure form (most journals use the ICMJE disclosure form), usually covering the last 36 months.

Funding statement: who paid, the grant number, and the role of the funder in design, data collection, analysis, writing and the decision to publish.

Running example: Paper 2 states its funder had no role in the design, data collection and analysis or manuscript preparation, an ICMJE requirement that is often forgotten (annotation \#39). Paper 1 states an internal hospital grant and no competing interests (page 12).

Ask: a drug company paid your travel to a congress last year. Do you declare it on a fluids paper? Expected: yes if it could be perceived as relevant. When in doubt, declare.
:::

## Data sharing: from 'on request' to open

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#0D7377"}
[From closed to open]{.neu-card-title}

- Not available
- 'Available on reasonable request' (Papers 1 and 2)
- Controlled-access repository
- Open repository with a DOI (permanent web identifier)
:::
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Before you share]{.neu-card-title}

- Consent form and ethics approval allow it
- Data de-identified
- Data dictionary and analysis code included
- Data-sharing statement in the paper
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Plan data sharing at the protocol stage: consent must allow it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: journals increasingly ask for a data-sharing statement. ICMJE requires one for clinical trials, and trials must describe their data-sharing plan when they register.

The ladder: not available. 'Available on reasonable request' (the weakest promise, used by both papers, pages 12 and 8). A controlled-access repository (researchers apply). An open repository with a DOI (digital object identifier, for fully de-identified data).

Before you share: the consent form and the ethics approval must allow it, data are de-identified, and you share the data dictionary and analysis code with the data so others can use them.

Link to Session 5: a clean data dictionary is what makes shared data usable.

Ask (call on two or three people, microphone on): what would you need to write in your consent form today so your data can be shared tomorrow? Expected: a sentence asking permission for de-identified data to be shared for future research.
:::

## AI in research and writing: what is allowed

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#2E8B57"}
[Allowed, with care]{.neu-card-title}

- Polish the language of your own text
- Brainstorm or summarise, then check every claim
- Disclose the tool, version and purpose
:::
::: {.neu-card style="--c:#C0392B"}
[Never]{.neu-card-title}

- List AI as an author
- Paste patient data or a confidential manuscript into a public AI tool
- Let AI invent references, data or images
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Use AI like a junior assistant: check everything, disclose it, keep patient data out.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: the current positions of ICMJE and COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics). AI tools cannot be authors, because they cannot take responsibility or be accountable for the work. Authors who use AI must disclose it (writing help usually in the Acknowledgements, use in data collection, analysis or figures in the Methods), and they remain fully responsible for every word, number and reference, including anything the tool produced.

Never paste identifiable patient data, or a manuscript you are reviewing, into a public AI tool: it breaches confidentiality, and reviewers are bound to keep manuscripts confidential.

AI tools can invent references that look real. Check every citation against PubMed.

Images: AI-generated or AI-altered images are not acceptable as data.

Always check the target journal's own AI policy in its Guide for Authors, because policies change.

Ask: a colleague asks a chatbot to 'write the discussion' and submits it unread. Which never points does this hit? Expected: invented references and an unaccountable text, and it is undisclosed.
:::

## Integrity scenarios: green, amber or red?

QUICK QUIZ · 5 min

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Scenarios: Session 7 exercise sheet, Part A (PDF sent before the session), also on the shared screen
- Vote in the poll: green (fine), amber (fine only if fixed or disclosed) or red (misconduct)
- One or two volunteers explain their vote with the microphone on
- We do 3 scenarios together now. The other 3 are homework
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Scenario 1

- Three day-3 fluid charts are lost. A resident enters the balances 'from memory'.
- Your colour?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone can name FFP, gift and ghost authorship, and the AI rules
:::

::: {.notes}
Quiz, whole class (20:25-20:30). Scenarios and answer key: Course/Practicals/s7\_exercises.md (Part A) and Course/Solutions/s7\_solutions.md.

Use three: 1 (missing data 'filled from memory': red, fabrication), 3 (head of department as last author without contributing: red, gift authorship, offer the Acknowledgements), 4 (AI polish of the English, checked and disclosed: green, the same chatbot fed the patient spreadsheet: red).

Run each as a three-option poll. Show the result, then ask one person from the largest and one from the smallest colour for a reason.

If the class is split, that is the teaching moment.
:::

Proposal builder 7 (20:30-20:45). Whole class. Share the Part B worksheet and fill it in live for the running example: a retrospective cohort of fluid balance and 28-day mortality in adults with septic shock in our ICU (model answers: Course/Solutions/s7\_solutions.md, Part B). For each answer, call on two or three people and type the best one.

Raise the typical problems as you go: (1) 'consent will be obtained' with no who, when or how (use the ICU flowchart). (2) retrospective chart reviews assuming no ethics review is needed (wrong: the committee decides and may grant a waiver). (3) recruitment numbers taken from the sample-size calculation instead of the unit's admissions. (4) CONSORT chosen for an observational study.

Homework: each participant writes Part 4 for their own proposal this week. The journal choice and reporting guideline are checked again in 8.2 next Saturday.

## 7.3  \|  35 minutes

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Writing the paper (I): Methods and Results
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
Write what you did and what you found, nothing more
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 7.3 (21:00-21:35). Nine slides (about 3.5 minutes each) and a 3-minute check at 21:32.

Every example comes from the course dataset (Q1, the primary question) or from the two papers.

The two worked examples are the heart of the block. Read them slowly with the class.
:::

## Write in a different order from the one readers read

::: {.neu-intro}
Readers read: Title, Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Writers start from the data.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[1 Tables]{.neu-step-label}

- Tables and figures: the story is in your data
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[2 Methods]{.neu-step-label}

- You know what you did
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[3 Results]{.neu-step-label}

- Describe your tables
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[4 Introduction]{.neu-step-label}

- Set up the question you answered
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[5 Discussion]{.neu-step-label}

- Answer, compare, explain
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#8A99A3"}
[6 Abstract, title]{.neu-step-label}

- Summarise the paper, name it last
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Start with your tables. Write the title last.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: readers go from title to abstract, introduction, methods, results and discussion. Writers should not. Start from the evidence: draft the tables and figures, then the Methods (it can be drafted from the protocol even before the data), then Results (describe the tables), then the Introduction (set up exactly the question you answered), then the Discussion, and only then the abstract and the title.

Why it works: each section is written from something that already exists, and the abstract and title summarise a paper that is finished, so they cannot promise more than the paper delivers.

Misconception: 'I must finish the introduction before I can start'. Many first-time writers stall on the introduction for months.

For the FLUID-ICU manuscript the tables already exist: they are in your results pack.
:::

## Methods: enough detail for someone to repeat it

::: {.neu-intro}
If a colleague could not redo your study from the Methods, add detail.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Who and where]{.neu-card-title}

- Design, setting, dates
- Eligibility criteria
- Ethics approval and consent
- Registration number
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[What was done]{.neu-card-title}

- Intervention or exposure in full
- Variables defined
- Paper 1: staff training, daily pharmacist check
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Outcomes and size]{.neu-card-title}

- One primary outcome: how and when
- Sample size: assumptions and source
- Paper 2: no sample-size statement
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Statistical analysis]{.neu-card-title}

- A method for each comparison
- Estimate matches the test
- Missing data, multiple comparisons
- Software and version
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The statistical paragraph names a method for every comparison you report.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: Methods = enough detail to repeat the study, in the order of the reporting checklist (CONSORT for trials or STROBE for observational studies).

Good practice: Paper 1 puts the ethics committee, approval number, consent procedure and funding inside the Methods (annotation \#13). Describes the intervention well enough to replicate: staff training, a daily pharmacist check, dilution charts in a supplement (\#16). Separates one primary outcome from secondary and safety outcomes (\#17). States the software and version (\#21). Paper 2 defines exactly which inputs and outputs make up fluid balance (\#13) and cites its cohort-profile paper instead of repeating it (\#12).

To fix: Paper 1 is a 'pilot' with an efficacy sample size whose assumptions (70 vs 40 ml/kg) were not met (\#18). It names a Mann-Whitney test but reports mean differences with CIs (\#19). About 40 secondary p-values with no word on multiplicity (\#20). Paper 2: 'caliper of 0.1' of what? How were missing covariates handled? Clustered by what? (\#15, \#17). No sample-size statement (\#19).

The annotated papers are in Course/Papers (annotation numbers refer to them).
:::

## Worked example: Methods for FLUID-ICU question 1

::: {.neu-intro}
One sentence per STROBE item (simulated data). STROBE = the reporting checklist for observational studies.
:::

- Items 4-6: We analysed FLUID-ICU, a prospective cohort of consecutive adults with sepsis admitted to four ICUs between January 2023 and December 2024.
- Item 7: The exposure was a positive cumulative fluid balance by ICU day 3 (fluid in minus fluid out over days 1-3, \> 0 ml/kg). The outcome was death from any cause within 28 days of ICU admission.
- Item 8: Data came from ICU charts on a standard case report form.
- Item 9: To address confounding by indication, we adjusted for severity and comorbidity pre-specified in the analysis plan.
- Item 10: All eligible patients in the cohort were included (no separate sample size).
- [Ethics (course version): This analysis used a simulated teaching dataset. No ethics approval or consent was required.]{style="color:#0B376C"}

::: {.notes}
Worked example (course dataset). Read each sentence and name its STROBE item.

All facts come from results pack Q1, section 2: prospective multicentre cohort, 4 ICUs, consecutive adults with sepsis, January 2023 to December 2024. Exposure = cumulative balance (in minus out, days 1-3) \> 0 ml/kg. Outcome = death within 28 days of ICU admission.

STROBE 10 (study size): for a fixed cohort we do not invent a sample-size calculation. We say all eligible patients were included.

The ethics sentence is specific to the course: FLUID-ICU is simulated, and every manuscript must say so.

Ask (call on two or three people, microphone on): which sentence would a reader need to repeat the study? Expected: the exposure definition (how fluid balance was calculated).
:::

## Worked example: the statistical-analysis paragraph

::: {.neu-intro}
STROBE item 12 for Q1: one sentence per decision, all chosen before seeing the data.
:::

- Baseline characteristics: mean (SD), median (IQR) or n (%), by balance group.
- 28-day mortality: chi-square test. Crude and adjusted odds ratios from logistic regression (age, SOFA score, lactate, vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, chronic kidney disease).
- Time to death: Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank test) and Cox regression with the same covariates. Proportional hazards checked.
- Effect modification by heart failure: an interaction term (pre-specified).
- Main analysis on complete cases. Missing lactate (15%) handled by multiple imputation (20 data sets) as a sensitivity analysis.
- Estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Analyses in R 4.6.

::: {.notes}
Worked example. This is STROBE item 12 written out for Q1 (results pack Q1, sections 2 and 4-5). SD = standard deviation. IQR = interquartile range. SOFA = Sequential Organ Failure Assessment.

Covariates: age, SOFA, lactate, vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, chronic kidney disease. All were pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan (SAP, Session 6), not chosen by looking at p-values.

Missing data: lactate missing in 93/620 (15.0%). Main analysis on complete cases (n = 527), multiple imputation (m = 20) as sensitivity.

Effect modification: heart failure, pre-specified.

Misconception: 'the statistics paragraph is for the statistician'. Reviewers read it first. Every number in the Results must be traceable to one sentence here.
:::

## Results: report, do not interpret

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[1  Participants first]{.neu-card-title}

- Screened, included, analysed, and why some were lost
- Paper 1: 1201 screened, 50 randomised, 48 analysed
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[2  Numbers with CIs]{.neu-card-title}

- Effect size with its 95% confidence interval (CI)
- Not 'p = 0.42, not significant'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[3  No interpretation]{.neu-card-title}

- Results report, the Discussion interprets
- Paper 2: results in the order of the aims
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[4  One home per number]{.neu-card-title}

- Key numbers in the text, details in the tables
- Paper 1: text and Table 1 disagree on creatinine
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Participants first, then each outcome as an effect size with its 95% CI.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four rules. 1) Participants first: how many were screened, included, analysed and why some were lost, with a flow diagram. Paper 1 has its CONSORT flow chart in the main text (annotations \#23, \#27). Paper 2 keeps it in the supplement although 79% of the registry was excluded (\#20).

2) Numbers with confidence intervals, not 'p = 0.42, NS'. Analysing 48 of 50 randomised patients is a modified intention-to-treat analysis and should be called that (\#24).

3) No interpretation in the Results. Paper 2 reports its results in the order of the aims, each with HR, CI and P, and no comment (\#25).

4) One home for each number: key numbers in the text, all details in the tables, and they must agree. Paper 1's text says creatinine was higher in the intervention group. Table 1 shows the opposite (\#25). Text-table contradictions are a classic rejection reason.

Tell participants: before you submit your draft, check every number in your text against your results pack.
:::

## Worked example: Results for FLUID-ICU question 1

::: {.neu-intro}
Participants, Table 1, outcome numbers, crude and adjusted estimates (simulated data).
:::

- Item 13: Of 620 patients enrolled, 618 had a day-3 fluid balance and were analysed, 527 had complete data for the adjusted model.
- Item 14: 373 (60.4%) had a positive balance. They were sicker: median SOFA 8 vs 6. Vasopressors 55.0% vs 24.9% (Table 1).
- Item 15: By day 28, 134 of 373 (35.9%) patients with a positive balance and 45 of 245 (18.4%) with a negative balance had died.
- Item 16: Crude OR 2.49 (95% CI 1.70 to 3.70), adjusted OR 1.62 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.59).
- Item 17: Multiple imputation: adjusted OR 1.70 (1.09 to 2.64). Adjusted Cox HR 1.46 (1.00 to 2.13).
- [No 'because', no 'significant', no 'suggests': numbers with 95% CIs only.]{style="color:#0B376C"}

::: {.notes}
Worked example. All numbers from Course/Data/key\_results.md (simulated data). OR = odds ratio. HR = hazard ratio.

Flow: 620 enrolled, 618 with a day-3 balance, 527 in the complete-case adjusted model (91 without lactate or age).

Positive balance 373/618 (60.4%). SOFA median 8 (6 to 10) vs 6 (4 to 8). Vasopressor 205/373 (55.0%) vs 61/245 (24.9%).

Deaths: 134/373 (35.9%) vs 45/245 (18.4%). Crude OR 2.49 (1.70 to 3.70), adjusted OR 1.62 (1.02 to 2.59), p 0.044. Sensitivity: multiple imputation OR 1.70 (1.09 to 2.64). Adjusted Cox HR 1.46 (1.00 to 2.13).

Point out what is not in the paragraph: no 'because', no 'significant', no explanation of why the OR shrank. That belongs to the Discussion next Saturday.

Poll: which STROBE item does the crude-and-adjusted sentence satisfy? Expected: 16.
:::

## Tables and figures that stand alone

![](images/figures/sat4/table_anatomy.png){.neu-fig}

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A reader should understand each table without reading the text.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: reviewers and clinicians read tables more carefully than text. A table must stand alone: a title that says what, in whom and when, n in every column header. Units and the summary statistic in each row. Footnotes defining abbreviations and missing data. The picture is Paper 1's Table 1, redrawn.

Good practice: Paper 1's Table 1 has n in each column, SD or IQR per row and no baseline p-values, which is correct for a randomised trial (annotation \#31). Paper 2's Table 1 adds SMDs (standardised mean differences) and footnotes with the number of patients with missing data (\#30). Its timeline figure has a self-contained legend (\#21).

Errors to avoid: sodium and potassium printed in umol per liter (should be mmol/L) in Paper 1 (\#30). A copy-pasted row in Paper 1's Table 2 (\#32). Wrong figure call-outs in Paper 1 (\#28, \#41). A vague table title (\#34). White-cell units written '\* 10\^3/L' in Paper 2 (\#30). Kaplan-Meier curves should show numbers at risk (Paper 2, \#31).

Link to Session 5: the publication-quality table rules. The FLUID-ICU Table 1 in each results pack already follows them.

Ask: what is wrong with a table titled 'Results'? Expected: it says nothing about what, who or when.
:::

## Worked example: FLUID-ICU Table 1 in one sentence

| Characteristic | Negative balance (n = 245) | Positive balance (n = 373) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Age, years, mean | 64.6 | 61.4 |
| SOFA score, median (IQR) | 6 (4 to 8) | 8 (6 to 10) |
| Vasopressor, n (%) | 61 (24.9%) | 205 (55.0%) |
| Mechanical ventilation, n (%) | 97 (39.6%) | 216 (57.9%) |
| Lactate, mmol/L, median (IQR) | 2.2 (1.4 to 3.0) | 2.9 (1.9 to 4.0) |
| Heart failure, n (%) | 54 (22.0%) | 43 (11.5%) |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Simulated data (results pack Q1, Table 1). SOFA = organ failure score. IQR = interquartile range. Sentence: 'Patients with a positive balance were sicker at baseline.'
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example: from Table 1 to one Results sentence (STROBE 14).

Model sentence: 'Patients with a positive balance were sicker at baseline (median SOFA 8 vs 6, vasopressors 55.0% vs 24.9%) and less often had heart failure (11.5% vs 22.0%).'

Teaching point: the Table 1 sentence describes, it does not test, so no p-values are needed (observational Table 1s often show SMDs instead).

Heart failure is lower in the positive group because clinicians give less fluid in heart failure: a good example of how treatment decisions shape the data.

The full Table 1 with missing-data rows is in each results pack.
:::

## STROBE for the FLUID-ICU paper: which item goes where

::: {.neu-intro}
FLUID-ICU is a cohort, so the paper follows STROBE. Numbers are STROBE item numbers.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Methods (items 4-12)]{.neu-card-title}

- 4  Design
- 5  Setting, dates
- 6  Participants
- 7  Variables
- 8  Data sources
- 9  Bias
- 10  Study size
- 12  Statistics, missing data
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Results (items 13-17)]{.neu-card-title}

- 13  Participants and flow
- 14  Descriptive data (Table 1)
- 15  Outcome data
- 16  Main results: crude and adjusted, 95% CI
- 17  Other analyses
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Write with the STROBE checklist open and tick each item as you write it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching point: FLUID-ICU is a cohort, so the paper follows STROBE (STrengthening the Reporting of OBservational studies in Epidemiology), cohort version. Item 11 (quantitative variables) is covered inside items 7 and 12.

Items most often forgotten: 9 (bias: say how you addressed confounding by indication, i.e. adjustment for severity), 10 (study size: for a fixed dataset say 'all eligible patients in the cohort were included'), 12 (missing data: how lactate was handled), 16 (give both crude and adjusted estimates, with the variables adjusted for).

The checklist is in the Session 7 exercise sheet (Part C) and on equator-network.org (demo next Saturday).

Poll: which item covers Table 1? Expected: 14 (descriptive data).
:::

## Check: Methods, Results or Discussion?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'We used logistic regression adjusted for SOFA score and age.'
- 'Of 620 patients enrolled, 618 had a day-3 fluid balance.'
- 'This may be because sicker patients received more fluid.'
- 'Lactate was missing in 15.0% of patients and was imputed.'
- '28-day mortality was higher with a positive balance (adjusted OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.59).'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Answers

- Methods
- Results (participants)
- Discussion (explains)
- Methods (how) and Results (how many)
- Results
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Check (21:32-21:35). One poll per sentence with three options: Methods, Results, Discussion. All numbers are FLUID-ICU Q1 results (key\_results.md).

Sentence 4 is the trick: how missing data were handled is Methods. How many were missing is Results.

Sentence 3 is the classic error: an interpretation slipped into the Results. Move it to the Discussion.
:::

## Manuscript workshop 1, part 1: we draft Q1 together

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 30 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- The instructor shares the manuscript template and results pack Q1
- Methods (15 min): you suggest each sentence aloud when called on. The instructor types the best one
- Results (12 min): participants, Table 1 sentence, crude and adjusted OR
- Number check (3 min): a volunteer reads each number against the pack
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Use

- Results pack Q1 (sent before the session)
- Manuscript template (Course/Templates)
- STROBE items 4-17
- The worked examples (slides)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** A class draft of the Q1 Methods and Results, shared as a PDF after the session
:::

::: {.notes}
Workshop Part 1 (21:35-22:05). Whole class. Start a visible timer and call each phase.

Methods in this order: design and setting, participants, variables (exposure, outcome, confounders), data sources and bias, study size, statistical analysis, ethics sentence (simulated data). Results: participants and flow, Table 1 sentence, outcome numbers, crude and adjusted OR, one sensitivity result.

Prompts to the class: 'Where is the statistical paragraph?' 'What did we adjust for?' 'Is there a number without a confidence interval?' 'Is there an adjective ("significant", "strong") that should be a number?' 'Is there any interpretation in our Results?'

Aim for about 300 words each. Save the class draft and share it as a PDF after the session: it is the model for everyone's own draft.
:::

The five questions

- Q1 Fluid balance and 28-day death
- Q2 Fluid balance and AKI (acute kidney injury)
- Q3 Fluid balance and ventilator-free days

- Q5 Fluid balance and ICU stay (survivors)

::: {.notes}
Workshop Part 2 (22:05-22:20). Individual, quiet writing. Keep the timer on screen and answer questions in the chat.

Participants who chose Q1 rewrite the class draft in their own words and add a figure or table. They do not copy it.

Question-specific points to post in the chat: Q4 reports both complete-case and imputed estimates. Q5 uses medians and IQR (survivors only). Q3: ventilator-free days are skewed and count death as zero, so check the summary.

Deadline for the Methods and Results draft: before Session 8 (by email). Next Saturday's workshop adds the Introduction, Discussion, Abstract and Title.

## Key words of Session 7

| Term | In plain words |
|:---|:---|
| Deferred consent | Enrol first in an emergency, ask consent as soon as possible (committee-approved) |
| Registration | Public record of a study before patient 1 (mandatory for trials) |
| FFP | Research misconduct: fabrication, falsification, plagiarism |
| ICMJE criteria | The four conditions every author must meet |
| Conflict of interest | Anything that could be seen to influence your judgement. Declare it |
| STROBE | Reporting checklist for observational studies: Methods items 4-12, Results 13-17 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Full glossary (English-Vietnamese): the PDF sent by email
:::

::: {.notes}
Key words (22:20-22:23). Show the term, call on someone to explain it with the microphone on, then reveal the right-hand column.

These are also the words most likely to appear in the post-course quiz next Saturday.
:::

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min

- A randomised trial of restrictive vs usual fluids in septic shock

- A clinical audit of fluid-balance charting against the unit standard

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Answers

- Must: a trial registry, before patient 1
- Should: PROSPERO
- Recommended, not required
- Audit: no research registration, local approval

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Extra check (1 minute + 1 minute answers). One poll per scenario with three options: must, should, not needed. Then reveal.

Scenario 4 starts a useful discussion: an audit compares practice with a standard and is usually approved through the quality office, not registered. If you plan to publish it as research, ask the ethics committee first (Session 1: research vs audit vs quality improvement).
:::

## IMRaD: the hourglass shape of every paper

![](images/figures/sat4/imrad_hourglass.png){.neu-fig}

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Introduction narrows to your question. Discussion widens back to practice.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra: Teaching point: almost every clinical paper follows IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion), framed by the title and abstract and closed by references and declarations.

Introduction: from what is known, to what is not known, to your question (a funnel). Methods: enough detail for someone else to repeat the study. Results: numbers, without opinions. Discussion: answer the question first, compare with other studies, state the limitations, then say what it means.

Running example: Paper 1's introduction is a textbook funnel in three paragraphs (pages 2-3), ending 'The primary objective was to assess the fluid balance after the first 5 days'. Its Discussion opens by answering that question (page 8).

Tip for the appraisal in Session 8: the hourglass tells you where to look. PICO is in the last paragraph of the Introduction, design and outcome in the Methods, the main effect in the first paragraph of the Results, limitations near the end of the Discussion.
:::

## CRediT: say who did what

::: {.neu-intro}
CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy): 14 standard roles that journals now ask for.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Some of the 14 roles]{.neu-card-title}

- Conceptualization
- Methodology
- Investigation
- Formal analysis
- Writing (original draft)
- Writing (review and editing)
- Supervision
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Paper 1 did it]{.neu-card-title}

- NB: Writing (original draft)
- CS: Methodology, Formal analysis
- SDB: Conceptualization, Supervision, Funding acquisition
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Your proposal]{.neu-card-title}

- Agree the author list now
- Write each person's roles
- Revisit before submission
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Transparent roles prevent gift and ghost authorship.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra: CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) is a list of 14 standard roles. It does not replace the ICMJE criteria. It makes each person's contribution visible.

Running example: Paper 1 (page 12) gives a CRediT statement. For example, the statistician is credited for Methodology and Formal analysis. Paper 2 (page 8) describes contributions in free text and states that all authors read and approved the final manuscript. That is acceptable, but CRediT is the format most journals now ask for.

Ask each participant to write, in their own proposal, who would be first author and who would do what. It prevents painful conversations later.

Question: in a hospital, who usually ends up as last author, and why? Expected: the senior supervisor. That is legitimate if they meet all four criteria, and a gift if they do not.
:::
